passages.title: Snowy Mountains
passages.author: John Gould Fletcher
passages.citation: “Snowy Mountains” by John Gould Fletcher—Public Domain

lines.text: Higher and still more high,
Palaces made for cloud,
Above the dingy city-roofs
Blue-white like angels with broad wings,
Pillars of the sky at rest
The mountains from the great plateau
Uprise.
But the world heeds them not;
They have been here now for too long a time.
The world makes war on them,
Tunnels their granite cliffs,
Splits down their shining sides,
Plasters their cliffs with soap-advertisements,
Destroys the lonely fragments of their peace.
Vaster and still more vast,
Peak after peak, pile after pile,
Wilderness still untamed,
To which the future is as was the past,
Barrier spread by Gods,
Sunning their shining foreheads,
Barrier broken down by those who do not need
The joy of time-resisting storm-worn stone,
The mountains swing along
The south horizon of the sky;
Welcoming with wide floors of blue-green ice
The mists that dance and drive before the sun.

questions.question: The description in the first stanza (lines 1–7) helps establish a central idea of the poem by

options.A: comparing the length of time the mountains have existed with the length of time the city has existed.
options.B: contrasting the grandeur of the mountains with the structures in the city below them.
options.C: implying that the mountains are a source of inspiration to the people in the city below.
options.D: suggesting that the mountains are larger than the people in the city realize.

questions.question: Which detail from the poem reflects the speaker’s view that people often fail to appreciate what is familiar?

options.B: “They have been here now for too long a time.” (line 9)
options.D: “To which the future is as was the past,” (line 18)

questions.question: How does isolating the word “Uprise” in line 7 affect the meaning of the poem?

options.A: It creates a contrast between the great plateau and the city buildings.
options.B: It reveals the similarity between the tall buildings in the city and the tall mountains on the horizon.
options.C: It creates a vision of the region before people developed the land.
options.D: It emphasizes that the mountains dominate the landscape.

questions.question:
In which **two** ways does the poet develop the speaker's point of view in the second stanza (lines 8–14)?

Select the **two** correct answers.

options.A: by describing the mountains' awe-inspiring size and strength
options.B: by comparing the various methods humans use to control nature
options.C: by criticizing the careless actions of humans that harm the natural environment
options.D: by demonstrating how the mountains and the people are able to benefit from each other
options.E: by depicting the unfortunate plight of the mountains with vivid details

questions.question:
Read lines 21–22 from the poem.

**Barrier broken down by those who do not need**
**The joy of time-resisting storm-worn stone,**

How do the lines help convey the speaker's point of view?

options.A: They suggest that the speaker wants to remove the obstacles that prevent others from experiencing the wonders of nature.
options.B: They reveal the speaker's opinion that some people are too busy to appreciate natural beauty.
options.C: They reflect the speaker's dismay that people destroy the natural landscape without understanding the ramifications of their actions.
options.D: They explain that the speaker is confident that nature will never be fully destroyed by people.

questions.question:
Read lines 23–26 from the poem.

**The mountains swing along**
**The south horizon of the sky;**
**Welcoming with wide floors of blue-green ice**
**The mists that dance and drive before the sun.**

The personification in these concluding lines of the poem suggests that the mountains are

options.A: gracious hosts who are untroubled by the actions of people.
options.C: lively entertainers who are amused by the everyday concerns of people.
options.D: too proud to reveal their pain.

questions.question:
Which quotations from the poem support the theme that nature's unspoiled beauty is splendid, and which quotations support the theme that human creations detract from natural wonder?

Move each answer to the correct box.

sort_items.text: “Above the dingy city-roofs / Blue-white like angels with broad wings,” (lines 3–4)
